Statistician working on uncertainty, extreme events, Bayesian spatial modelling, dependence, astrostatistics and scientific computing. Based in Brasília, Brazil.

I study extreme events, spatial structure and uncertainty through statistical inference and simulation. My work connects environmental and atmospheric questions with a growing research direction in astrostatistics.
How can we turn uncertainty about the unknown into clear, accessible science?

I trained in Statistics at the University of Brasília, drawn to a way of reasoning about uncertainty that could travel across scientific questions. Probability and inference remain my foundation, even as the systems I study change.

My first research asked what could be recovered when observations were missing. Predictive modelling and simulation led me to a harder version of that question: what can we infer when the observations that matter most are scarce or extreme?

That question now connects my work on spatial extremes, dependence and environmental data with solar irradiance and astrostatistics. Astronomy has long been a personal interest; it is increasingly a place where I can contribute quantitatively, alongside the environmental questions that continue to shape my research.
Four connected research directions, moving between mathematical questions and the physical systems that make them consequential.

How I tend to think about a scientific problem
I often begin by asking what the observations can support, which assumptions the answer depends on, and what remains uncertain.
Simulation and diagnostics help me examine recovery, calibration and failure modes, especially when the observations offer few ways to check an assumption.
The scientific question and the measurement process help shape my modelling choices. Different problems call for different tools and collaborations.

Start from imperfect observations, look for the structure behind them, and be explicit about what the model still does not capture.

Missing data can hinder statistical analyses that rely on complete datasets. In work coauthored with Eduardo Yoshio Nakano, I explored how regression-based imputation can help, using simulated datasets to compare single and multiple imputation, measures of central tendency, and predictive modelling.

We examined the proportion of missing data, the nature of the incomplete variables, and how many variables were affected. We also compared imputation with ignoring or deleting incomplete observations. The study points to the importance of matching the method to the nature and extent of missing data, and brings together the literature and simulation results to offer practical guidance for researchers.

My undergraduate research compares mode imputation and logistic-regression imputation for a binary variable in a horseshoe-crab dataset. Repeated simulations introduce different proportions of missing values, allowing us to examine recovery accuracy and the prediction error of a subsequent linear model for shell width.

The study found more accurate recovery of the binary values and lower variability in prediction error with logistic-regression imputation. Mode imputation produced a slightly lower mean prediction error in these simulations.

Dependence, joint return levels, and environmental extremes
Research on multivariate dependence and compound extremes, including the joint behaviour of maximum temperature and minimum relative humidity.

Many high-impact events are not adequately described by one variable at a time. Temperature and humidity, for example, can combine into regimes whose joint behaviour matters more than either marginal distribution alone. Copulas provide a way to model that dependence separately from the marginals while preserving probabilistic coherence.
Earlier temperature–humidity work, presented at RBras/SEAGRO 2025. The complete poster preserves the methods and figures in their original context.

One project estimates joint return levels for maximum temperature and minimum relative humidity by combining copulas with an extreme-value framework for bimodal data. A related collaboration studies conditional copula representations and extremal bounds for multivariate statistical functionals.

Dependence modelling is the bridge between several of my projects: compound climate extremes, joint solar–atmospheric behaviour, spatial covariance in the MSc thesis, and more general questions about how information is shared across variables, locations and physical processes.

A methodological project connecting the missing-data questions of my undergraduate work with the extreme-value problems that became central during the MSc.

My BSc thesis used predictive modelling and simulation to compare single and multiple imputation strategies across controlled missing-data scenarios. Later, after moving into Extreme Value Theory, a natural question returned:
what happens to conventional imputation procedures when the data contain extreme observations?
Earlier work: simulation comparison presented at coBIPE 2024. This figure belongs to the undergraduate research direction, not the 2026 preprint.

I use Monte Carlo simulation and MICE in R to compare multiple imputation methods in regression settings, with and without extreme values. The comparisons examine how sample size, missingness and the fitted model affect predictive performance. Linear regression imputation performed best overall by cross-validated mean squared error in the studied scenarios; that result is not a universal ranking of methods.
Why it matters to my research

This work makes the continuity in my trajectory explicit. Missing data did not disappear when I started studying extremes; the original question became harder. It also reinforced a methodological habit that appears throughout my work: use synthetic-data experiments to understand what a procedure recovers before trusting it on observations where the truth is unknown.

A project using Extreme Value Theory to study extreme behaviour in solar spectral irradiance measured by NASA’s SORCE mission, bringing statistical methodology into dialogue with physical observations.

Astronomy had been part of my academic interests long before I had a statistical toolkit strong enough to contribute quantitatively. During the MSc, work with solar irradiance became one of the first places where those directions genuinely met: a physical observational record, questions about extreme behaviour, and methods I could interrogate statistically rather than treat as a black box.

The preprint models extremes of daily logarithmic irradiance changes in the 2005–2019 SORCE/XPS record using GEV distributions. Maximum likelihood fits are checked against probability weighted moments. Long return periods require extrapolation beyond this finite record; reported measurement uncertainty informs interpretation but is not propagated through the likelihood.
Related solar and atmospheric research produced posters and oral presentations, including an international talk in the astrophysics applications track of

The project marks a shift from treating a physical dataset as merely another application toward asking how the measurement process, scientific context, uncertainty and statistical model interact. That is the direction I want to deepen in astrostatistics, cosmology and other quantitative physical sciences.

The Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution is widely used in the modelling of spatial extremes, but it may be limited when representing data from complex systems subject to multiple occurrence regimes. In this work, a Bayesian hierarchical geostatistical model is proposed for spatial extreme values with Bimodal Generalized Extreme Value (BGEV) marginal distribution, allowing the accommodation of bimodality and greater marginal flexibility. In the proposed model, latent predictors associated with the four parameters of the BGEV distribution are specified through Gaussian spatial structures, with appropriate transformations to preserve the parametric constraints of the distribution. Inference is performed using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, employing the No-U-Turn Sampler algorithm implemented in the Stan software, accessed through R. The performance of the model is evaluated through a simulation study and an application to quarterly extremes of relative humidity deficit in the Amazon region. The results indicate the potential of the methodology for modelling spatial extreme data with bimodal behavior, while preserving a hierarchical structure capable of representing spatial heterogeneity in the marginal parameters.
